What is Gromov hyperbolicity
---
## Assistant
Gromov hyperbolicity measures how much a metric space behaves like a tree.
For a graph, it answers:
Are shortest paths arranged like branching hierarchy, or like flat grid geometry?
A graph is Gromov-hyperbolic if its geodesic triangles are uniformly thin.
Core idea: thin triangles
Take any three points x,y,zx,y,zx,y,z in a metric space. Connect them by shortest paths, forming a triangle.
In Euclidean space, triangles can be fat.
In a tree, triangles are maximally thin: the three paths share a central trunk.
A space is δ\deltaδ-hyperbolic if every side of every geodesic triangle stays within distance δ\deltaδ of the other two sides.
∀ Δ(x,y,z),[x,y]⊆Nδ([x,z]∪[z,y])\forall\ \Delta(x,y,z),\quad [x,y]\subseteq N_\delta([x,z]\cup[z,y])∀ Δ(x,y,z),[x,y]⊆Nδ​([x,z]∪[z,y])
Here:
[x,y][x,y][x,y] is a shortest path from xxx to yyy;
Nδ(A)N_\delta(A)Nδ​(A) means the δ\deltaδ-neighborhood of AAA;
δ\deltaδ is the hyperbolicity constant.
Smaller δ\deltaδ means more tree-like.
δ=0\delta = 0δ=0
means the space is essentially tree-like.
For graphs
Given a graph GGG, use shortest-path distance:
d(u,v)=length of shortest path from u to vd(u,v)=\text{length of shortest path from }u\text{ to }vd(u,v)=length of shortest path from u to v
Then GGG is Gromov-hyperbolic if all shortest-path triangles are thin.
So:

A tree has no “fat” regions. A grid does. That is the main distinction.

There is also a very useful distance-only definition.
For any four points a,b,c,da,b,c,da,b,c,d, compute:
